pages.text: After football, Ayamga was very thirsty. He saw an open pot of water in the yard and scooped a cup with his hands. The pot had been left uncovered, and flies had been landing on it.
sentences: After football, Ayamga was very thirsty.
He saw an open pot of water in the yard and scooped a cup with his hands.
The pot had been left uncovered, and flies had been landing on it.
pages.alt: In a warm afternoon courtyard after football, sweaty Ayamga scoops water from an uncovered clay water pot while a couple of small flies hover near the rim.

pages.text: That night, Ayamga’s tummy hurt. He ran to the washroom again and again. Mama Kuuire felt his forehead. “You have lost a lot of water from your body,” she said. “We must give it back.”
sentences: That night, Ayamga’s tummy hurt.
He ran to the washroom again and again.
Mama Kuuire felt his forehead.
“You have lost a lot of water from your body,” she said.
“We must give it back.”
pages.alt: In a warm lamp-lit room, Ayamga sits on a wooden chair holding his tummy with a tired face while Mama Kuuire gently touches his forehead.

pages.text: Mama Kuuire opened a packet of oral rehydration salts, called ORS, and mixed it with clean, safe water just as the health worker had taught her. “Take small sips,” she said. “This helps your body get back the water it lost.”
sentences: Mama Kuuire opened a packet of oral rehydration salts, called ORS, and mixed it with clean, safe water just as the health worker had taught her.
“Take small sips,” she said.
“This helps your body get back the water it lost.”
pages.alt: At a clean wooden table, Mama Kuuire stirs a clear glass of safe water and gently helps Ayamga take small sips from a clean cup.

pages.text: In the morning, Mama Kuuire took Ayamga to the clinic. The health worker said, “You were right to come. Unsafe water can carry germs that cause a bad tummy. Keep giving ORS and come to us if it does not get better.”
sentences: In the morning, Mama Kuuire took Ayamga to the clinic.
The health worker said, “You were right to come.
Unsafe water can carry germs that cause a bad tummy.
Keep giving ORS and come to us if it does not get better.”
pages.alt: Inside a bright, clean Ghanaian community clinic, a smiling nurse in a teal uniform speaks warmly with Mama Kuuire and Ayamga.

pages.text: “How do we stop this?” asked Mama Kuuire. “Use clean drinking water. Keep it in a covered container. Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the washroom,” said the health worker. “Always use a clean cup.”
sentences: “How do we stop this?” asked Mama Kuuire.
“Use clean drinking water.
Keep it in a covered container.
Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the washroom,” said the health worker.
“Always use a clean cup.”
pages.alt: The nurse points to a clean blue water container fitted with a tight lid and tap beside a bar of soap and a clean cup.

pages.text: That evening, Ayamga felt better. At home, the family covered the pot, washed their hands with soap and used a clean cup. “I will not drink from an open pot again,” said Ayamga.
sentences: That evening, Ayamga felt better.
At home, the family covered the pot, washed their hands with soap and used a clean cup.
“I will not drink from an open pot again,” said Ayamga.
pages.alt: In golden evening light in their tidy compound, a smiling, healthy Ayamga and Mama Kuuire wash their hands with soap beside a neatly covered water pot.
